analysis.one_liner: Requires federal agencies to document job and wage impacts and weigh alternatives before issuing new regulations.
analysis.headline: The bill died in the House Judiciary Committee without a single cosponsor, hearing, or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would rewrite the process federal agencies must follow before issuing new rules. Agencies would have to base every factual finding on evidence, formally consider the option of doing nothing, and calculate costs and benefits — including projected effects on jobs and wages in specific industries. Rules projected to cut employment or weekly wages by 1% or more in any industry, or to reduce employment in any industry with unemployment above 5%, would be flagged as 'negative-impact' rules and face extra scrutiny. Supporters frame this as accountability for regulators; critics say it stacks the deck so protective rules are slower and easier to challenge in court.
analysis.who_benefits: Businesses that face federal regulation — manufacturers, energy companies, financial firms, and other regulated industries — would gain because agencies would have to clear a much higher analytical bar before issuing rules, and the extra findings would give companies more grounds to challenge rules in court. Small businesses would get expanded impact analyses of how rules affect them.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Regulated industries and their trade groups

how_it_helps.text: Agencies would have to base all preliminary and final factual determinations on evidence, a discipline supporters say makes regulation more accurate and accountable.

Before issuing a rule, agencies would have to formally consider the alternative of no federal response, amending or rescinding existing rules, and leaving the problem to states — options that reduce the volume of new regulation.

Agencies would have to estimate a rule's net gain or loss in domestic jobs, effects on wages, economic growth, and impacts on low-income populations, and flag any rule projected to cut employment or weekly wages by 1% or more in a given industry.

analysis.who_pays: Workers and consumers who rely on federal rules — workplace safety standards, environmental limits, consumer and financial protections — would bear the cost if rules they depend on are delayed, weakened, or blocked by the new analytical hurdles. Government agencies would also bear added analytical costs, slowing their work across the board.
analysis.who_pays_short: Workers and consumers protected by regulation

drawbacks.text: The new requirements would apply to every rulemaking, so protections unrelated to jobs — such as safety or health rules — could be delayed or abandoned while agencies compile the mandated analyses, and the mandated consideration of 'no Federal response' pushes agencies toward inaction.

Projecting a rule's effect on employment and wages in specific industries years into the future is inherently uncertain, so agencies could be second-guessed in court for projections that prove wrong, giving regulated parties a new tool to tie rules up in litigation.

Supporters would argue the bill responds to a real problem: agencies sometimes issue costly rules built on thin analysis, and businesses and their employees absorb compliance costs that cost-benefit review is meant to surface.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offers real procedural accountability — evidence-based findings and honest cost accounting are reasonable demands — but it applies the same heavy process to every rule and hard-wires 'jobs and wages' projections as a trigger for extra scrutiny. That structure favors regulated industries over the people rules are written to protect, and the delays and litigation exposure would fall hardest on workers and consumers who depend on timely protections.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Judiciary Committee on the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Tim Burchett introduced the bill on August 14, 2020, and it was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary the same day.
No further action was taken for the rest of the 116th Congress, which ended January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, the status quo held: federal agencies keep their existing rulemaking process, and businesses seeking a higher bar for new regulation did not get one. Workers and consumers who rely on federal rules are better off than they would have been if it had passed.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Workers and consumers protected by existing rules

for.name: Rep. Tim Burchett
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on August 14, 2020; it was his sole action on it.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee
against.role: Committee of referral (chaired by Rep. Jerrold Nadler, D-NY)
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a hearing or markup; it sat in committee until the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and the bill drew no cosponsors of either party, so no partisan split can be measured; a single Republican sponsor sent it to a committee controlled by Democrats.

industries.industry: Regulated industries generally (manufacturers, energy producers, financial firms, and other businesses subject to federal rules)
industries.note: If passed, the bill would have made new federal rules harder and slower to issue by requiring extensive evidence, alternatives analysis, and job and wage projections, with a special flag for rules projected to cut industry employment or wages by 1% or more. The industry's gain — fewer, delayed, and more litigable rules — would come at the cost of the protections those rules provide workers and consumers.

The bill would expand the analysis agencies must do of rules' impacts on small entities, and small firms often bear compliance costs disproportionately. But the benefit depends on rules actually being softened, which the bill does not itself require.
